transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
Stocks have extended their rally following Jensen Huang's return to NVIDIA as CEO.
Asia markets largely advanced after Wall Street surged Monday,
and President Trump is taking credit saying he made the deal.
But while investors are welcoming Huang's return, not everyone is celebrating.
Maryland Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen says he believes Trump is motivated by money, not national security.
The concern is that it is undermining our national security interests.
After all, high-end ships can be used by the military in China, and it's completely, it's just completely hypocritical.
Van Hollen is challenging New York Senator Chuck Schumer for the Democratic Leaders Post.
NVIDIA's board announced Huang's return Monday, less than two weeks after he resigned amid an alleged Chinese spy scandal.
The Commerce Department, meanwhile, has added to a blacklist Singapore-based Megaspeed,
the cloud company at the center of the scandal, and also separately added a Singapore subsidiary of Alibaba.
A federal appeals court has revived President Trump's bid to move his hush money case from state to federal court.
The decision keeps the door open to the president's efforts to erase his criminal conviction.
Here's NPR's Ryan Lucas.
A jury in New York State found Trump guilty in 2024 of falsifying business records to hide hush money payments
made to adult film star Stormy Daniels.
Trump has fought his criminal conviction, arguing in part that the case should be moved from state court to federal court
where he could argue presidential immunity.
Now, a three-judge panel on the Second Circuit Court of Appeals has ruled that a district court judge had aired in his decision
that Trump's state case categorically couldn't be moved to federal court after his conviction.
The appeals court sent the matter back to the district court to consider Trump's removal request again.
Ryan Lucas, NPR News, Washington.
Overseas now to northern Gaza, where an Israeli airstrike has killed an employee of the UN Agency for Palestinian Refugees, or ANRA.
This marks the agency's 396th death of a staff member since the war began three years ago.
And Pirazan Asbaba reports.
52-year-old Adel Al-Halo was killed in a strike that UNRWA says hit close to the gates of a water well in the Jabali refugee camp.
Al-Halo, Agarb, and other staff members were carrying out their regular duties at the well.
All wearing clearly marked blue UNRWA vests.
Israel did not immediately comment on the incident.
The well serves thousands of displaced families in the area, where access to safe water is increasingly a public health concern.
Gaza's Health Ministry told NPR that hospitals and clinics are seeing a sharp rise in meningitis cases among children.
Ten recent deaths have been linked mainly to contaminated water wells and damaged sewage systems.
And Asbaba and Pirazan use Gaza.
This is NPR News.
The status of a plan to detonate several tons of degraded bomb-making material at an ammunition plant in Iowa is not clear.
After a federal appeals court cleared the way for the detonation, the U.S. Army said it would happen Wednesday morning.
But President Trump has also demanded that Iowa's Democratic governor-elect Rob Sand weigh in.
Sand does not take office until January, but he called for transparency, and in a social media post said that the Trump administration should make the decision, given that it brought people in to do the job months ago.
In his own social media post, Trump said he would blame sand for any and all death or destruction if the material explodes spontaneously.
License hunters and trappers killed more than 400 bobcats in Indiana this month, exceeding the state quota and ending the season early.
Ethan Sandwise, member station WFIU, reports a hunter's controversial industry where bobcats were recently endangered.
"Once nearly hunted to extinction in the state, bobcat numbers are now stable," says Jerry Ann Albers, fur bearer and game bird program leader at the Indiana Department of Natural Resources.
"They're a great success story and they've recovered well, and obviously we are going to keep that in mind. The people of Indiana value bobcats and we don't want them to go extinct again."
It's the second hunt since bobcats were removed from the endangered species list in Indiana in 2005.
The season's quota was 150 higher than last year, more than the department thinks the population can sustain in the long term.
But it says it will adjust next year's limit based on a post-season survey.
For NPR News, I'm Ethan Sandwise in Bloomington, Indiana.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: Stocks rally after NVIDIA board names Jensen Huang CEO again, Trump claims credit for deal
Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen criticizes Trump over Nvidia chip deal, challenges Schumer for leadership
Commerce Department blacklists Singapore-based Megaspeed and an Alibaba Singapore subsidiary
Second Circuit revives Trump's bid to move hush money conviction case to federal court
Israeli airstrike in northern Gaza kills UNRWA staff member Adel Al-Halo near Jabali camp water well
Army plans Wednesday detonation of degraded bomb-making material at Iowa ammunition plant; Trump and Governor-elect Rob Sand spar
Indiana bobcat hunters kill over 400 animals, exceeding quota and ending season early
